old: Its name once belonged to one company alone, until a postwar ruling let the word loose for everyone to use.
The name is a shortened nod to an acid found in a flowering plant, dressed up with a chemical process called acetylation.
It shares its trademark fate with heroin — both were German brand names stripped of protection after World War I.
clues: This everyday medicine began life as a protected German trade name, and it only became an ordinary English word after World War I stripped that protection away in the United States.
A white tablet taken for headaches, fever and inflammation, and in a small daily dose to help prevent heart attacks; unlike ibuprofen or paracetamol, it thins the blood.
The classic doctor's advice: "Take two of these and call me in the morning." Heroin is its sibling, another German trademark that slipped into ordinary use after the war.
